title: Explain the Purpose of Mitigation Techniques Used to Secure the Enterprise

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: After an organization identifies threats and vulnerabilities, it needs controls that reduce the likelihood or impact of an attack. A mitigation is a safeguard used to reduce risk.
Mitigations can prevent attacks, limit how far an attacker can move, reduce exposure, protect data, detect activity, or remove vulnerabilities.
Use this decision path: identify the risk first, then choose the mitigation that most directly reduces that risk.
sections.callout: Find the weakness or threat first, then choose the control that directly reduces it.

sections.title: Segmentation
paragraphs: Segmentation divides a network or environment into smaller sections based on function, trust, sensitivity, or business need.
A compromise in one segment should not automatically provide access to every other part of the environment. Segmentation limits lateral movement, contains incidents, and reduces exposure.

entries.title: Segmentation
paragraphs: Use segmentation when the organization needs planned boundaries between groups of systems or networks.
entries.memoryHook: One compromised neighborhood should not open the whole kingdom.
entries.recognitionCue: Separate networks or systems to limit movement and incident spread -> Segmentation

sections.title: Access Control
paragraphs: Access control determines who or what may use a resource and which actions are allowed. Objective 2.5 specifically distinguishes access control lists from permissions.

entries.title: Access Control
paragraphs: Access control is the broad mitigation used to restrict access to resources.
entries.memoryHook: Who or what may enter, and what may happen after entry?
entries.recognitionCue: Restrict subjects and allowed resource use -> Access control

entries.title: Access Control List (ACL)
paragraphs: An ACL is an ordered set of rules that permits or denies access. ACLs can control network traffic, file access, and other system resources.
entries.memoryHook: A rule list decides who or what gets through.
entries.recognitionCue: Ordered permit-and-deny rules -> ACL

entries.title: Permissions
paragraphs: Permissions define the actions an authorized user or process may perform, such as read, write, modify, execute, or delete.
entries.memoryHook: You are allowed in, but what are you allowed to do?
entries.recognitionCue: Assigned rights define allowed operations -> Permissions

table.caption: Access-control distinction
rows: Which rule permits or denies access?
What may an authorized subject do?

sections.title: Application Allow List
paragraphs: An application allow list identifies the applications approved to run. Software that is not on the approved list is blocked.

entries.title: Application Allow List
paragraphs: Use an allow list when the requirement is to restrict execution to explicitly approved software.
entries.memoryHook: Only invited software gets to run.
entries.recognitionCue: Only specifically approved applications may execute -> Application allow list

sections.title: Isolation
paragraphs: Isolation strongly separates a particular system or resource from the rest of the environment. Organizations may isolate infected endpoints, vulnerable systems, suspicious devices, or sensitive workloads.

entries.title: Isolation
paragraphs: Use isolation when a specific system must be quarantined so it cannot affect other resources.
entries.memoryHook: Segmentation creates neighborhoods; isolation creates quarantine.
entries.recognitionCue: Separate a suspicious or compromised system from others -> Isolation

table.caption: Segmentation and isolation
rows: Planned division of an environment into controlled areas
Strong separation of one particular system or resource

sections.title: Patching
paragraphs: Patching applies vendor fixes to applications, operating systems, firmware, and other software. Security patches commonly correct known vulnerabilities.

entries.title: Patching
paragraphs: Use patching when a known vulnerability has an available vendor fix.
entries.memoryHook: Known vulnerability plus available vendor fix means patch it.
entries.recognitionCue: Install an available fix for a known vulnerability -> Patching

sections.title: Encryption
paragraphs: Encryption protects data from unauthorized disclosure by converting it into unreadable ciphertext. It can protect information at rest and in transit.

entries.title: Encryption
paragraphs: Choose encryption when the risk is unauthorized reading or disclosure of sensitive information.
entries.memoryHook: Stolen data should still be unreadable.
entries.recognitionCue: Protect the confidentiality of data -> Encryption

sections.title: Monitoring
paragraphs: Monitoring observes systems and activity for suspicious or unexpected behavior. It can cover logs, network traffic, endpoints, authentication, and resource usage.

entries.title: Monitoring
paragraphs: Monitoring primarily provides visibility and detection. It does not necessarily block the activity it observes.
entries.recognitionCue: Observe systems or events to identify suspicious activity -> Monitoring

sections.title: Least Privilege
paragraphs: Least privilege gives a user, application, or process only the access required to perform its job. Unnecessary privileges increase the damage an account or process can cause if compromised.

entries.title: Least Privilege
paragraphs: A help-desk employee may need permission to reset passwords without receiving full domain-administrator access.
entries.memoryHook: Only what you need, nothing extra.
entries.recognitionCue: Grant only the minimum required permissions -> Least privilege

sections.title: Configuration Enforcement
paragraphs: Configuration enforcement keeps systems aligned with approved security settings and secure baselines. It helps prevent configuration drift, unauthorized settings, and inconsistent controls.

entries.title: Configuration Enforcement
paragraphs: Use configuration enforcement when approved settings must remain applied over time.
entries.memoryHook: These are the approved settings, and they stay that way.
entries.recognitionCue: Require systems to maintain approved secure settings -> Configuration enforcement

sections.title: Decommissioning
paragraphs: Decommissioning securely removes systems, devices, applications, or services that are no longer needed. It can include removing accounts and network access, sanitizing data, updating documentation, and retiring hardware or software.

entries.title: Decommissioning
paragraphs: Isolation leaves a system in place but separated. Decommissioning permanently retires it.
entries.memoryHook: If the organization is finished with it, remove it safely.
entries.recognitionCue: Securely retire an unneeded system, account, or service -> Decommissioning

sections.title: Hardening Techniques
paragraphs: Hardening reduces a system's attack surface by strengthening its configuration and removing unnecessary exposure. Leave only the access, software, services, and functions that the system actually needs.

entries.title: Hardening Techniques
paragraphs: Hardening is the broad group of configuration and protection steps used to make a system more resistant to attack.
entries.recognitionCue: Strengthen configuration and remove unnecessary exposure -> Hardening

entries.title: Encryption as Hardening
paragraphs: Encryption can be part of a hardening plan when sensitive data must be protected from unauthorized disclosure.
entries.recognitionCue: Use cryptography to harden sensitive data against disclosure -> Encryption

sections.title: Endpoint Protection
paragraphs: Endpoint protection places security directly on a workstation, laptop, or server. It can detect malware, block malicious behavior, and remove threats.

entries.title: Endpoint Protection
paragraphs: Use endpoint protection when the control must detect or block threats directly on the host.
entries.memoryHook: Put protection directly on the endpoint.
entries.recognitionCue: Install security software that detects or blocks endpoint threats -> Endpoint protection

sections.title: Host-Based Firewall and HIPS
paragraphs: Both controls protect an individual host, but they focus on different activity.

entries.title: Host-Based Firewall
paragraphs: A host-based firewall filters network traffic entering or leaving one computer or server.
entries.recognitionCue: Filter network traffic directly on an endpoint -> Host-based firewall

entries.title: Host-Based Intrusion Prevention System (HIPS)
paragraphs: A HIPS monitors activity on an individual host and can actively block suspicious behavior based on rules or behavior.
entries.memoryHook: Watch the host and stop suspicious actions.
entries.recognitionCue: Host-level monitoring plus active prevention -> HIPS

table.caption: Host-level protection comparison
rows: Network traffic entering and leaving one host
Host activity with active prevention of suspicious behavior

sections.title: Disable Unused Ports and Protocols
paragraphs: Unused ports, services, and protocols create unnecessary communication paths and increase the attack surface. If the organization does not need them, disable them.

entries.title: Disabling Ports and Protocols
paragraphs: This hardening step removes communication paths that have no approved business purpose.
entries.memoryHook: Do not leave an unused door open.
entries.recognitionCue: Turn off unnecessary communication paths and services -> Disable ports and protocols

sections.title: Default Passwords and Unnecessary Software
paragraphs: Default credentials and unneeded applications create avoidable exposure. Both should be removed before they become an attack path.

entries.title: Default Password Changes
paragraphs: Vendor-supplied credentials may be publicly documented, shared across devices, and known to attackers. Replace them before production use.
entries.recognitionCue: Replace vendor-supplied credentials before deployment -> Default password changes

entries.title: Removal of Unnecessary Software
paragraphs: Every installed application can introduce vulnerabilities, services, and dependencies. Removing software the system does not need reduces its attack surface.
entries.memoryHook: Attackers cannot exploit software that is not installed.
entries.recognitionCue: Uninstall unused applications to reduce attack surface -> Remove unnecessary software

sections.title: Recognition Cues
paragraphs: Identify the risk in the scenario first, then select the control that most directly addresses it.
bullets: Permit or deny access through ordered rules -> ACL
Control what an authorized user may do -> Permissions
Only approved programs may run -> Application allow list
Fix a known vulnerability with an available vendor update -> Patching
Keep systems on an approved baseline -> Configuration enforcement
Retire an old system securely -> Decommissioning
Protect a host directly -> Endpoint protection
Control traffic on one host -> Host-based firewall
Actively block suspicious host behavior -> HIPS
Unused service or protocol -> Disable it

sections.title: Objective 2.5 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Several mitigations may reduce risk, but choose the one that most directly addresses the problem described.
Segmentation creates planned boundaries across the environment. Isolation quarantines a particular system or resource.
An ACL applies permit-and-deny rules. Permissions define what an authorized subject may do.
An application allow list controls which software may execute. Access control is the broader restriction of resource use.
Monitoring observes and detects. A HIPS observes host activity and can actively prevent suspicious behavior.
Patching fixes known software vulnerabilities. Configuration enforcement maintains approved settings.
If no patch exists yet, patching is not immediately available. Temporary mitigation may require isolation, disabling vulnerable functionality, configuration changes, or additional monitoring.
sections.callout: The best mitigation is the control that most directly satisfies the scenario's security requirement.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
paragraphs: Use this final sheet to connect each requirement to its most direct mitigation.
bullets: Permit or deny through rules -> ACL
Run only approved software -> Application allow list
Maintain a secure baseline -> Configuration enforcement
Filter traffic on one host -> Host-based firewall
Unused port or protocol -> Disable it

miniCheck.intro: Choose the mitigation that most directly addresses each risk.
miniCheck.prompt: A workstation shows signs of active malware and must be prevented from communicating with other systems. A newly installed network appliance still uses the vendor-supplied administrator credential.
miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. Isolation immediately quarantines the compromised workstation, while replacing the vendor-supplied credential removes a known default-access weakness from the appliance.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Identify the control that quarantines one affected device, then identify the hardening step that removes a publicly known factory credential. Review Isolation and Default Passwords, then try again.
